sections.name: Heart Container (Heart)
sections.card:
Summary: A healing item that takes damage off whoever grabs it. The first game just calls it Heart, and there it wipes out all of your damage, down to 0%.
Uses: It appears in the air and drifts down slowly, which in the first game leaves a gap in which fighters battle over its landing spot. After someone has taken it, the healing carries on even if they are hit during it.
Tips: Collect enough of them in a single match for the Heartthrob bonus, which pays 17,000 points in the first game and 8,000 in its Japanese release.

sections.name: Maxim Tomato
sections.card:
Summary: A red tomato marked with a black M, which takes damage off whoever picks it up. In the first game it clears 100% of your damage; the later games only clear 50%.
Uses: In the first game, hits you take during the healing do no damage. Hyrule Castle never gets Maxim Tomatoes.
Tips: Eat enough of them in one match for the Vegetarian bonus: 9,000 points in the first game, 5,000 in its Japanese release. Turn off every item but the Maxim Tomato and the containers that drop onto the stage will hold nothing.

sections.name: Starman (Super Star)
sections.card:
Summary: A star that bounces around and gives whoever touches it ten seconds of invincibility. It was called the Starman in the first game, and kept that name until Brawl's PAL release and Smash 4's NTSC release.
Uses: It hops across the stage in big arcs, rebounding from platforms and walls, and it can drop off the edge if nobody catches it soon enough. Touching an enemy while invincible does them no harm. The fighter glitters, and a dedicated tune takes over from the stage music until the effect ends.
Tips: In the first game every item carries a little triangle above it except this one. In the series, invincibility does not save a fighter who falls off the stage: they can still be KO'd.

sections.name: Beam Sword
sections.card:
Summary: A sword modelled on the lightsaber, and nicknamed after it, that you swing for stronger hits or throw at opponents. Among the battering items, it travels the farthest when thrown.
Uses: Holding it turns your forward smash, dash attack, forward tilt and neutral attack into item swipes. In the first game they deal 25%, 16%, 18% and 12%, in that order.
Tips: A thrown Beam Sword deals from 13% to 20%, depending on which throw. Getting hit while you hold it can make you drop it: in the first game the odds are the hit's damage over 60, so a hit of 6% gives a 10% chance.

sections.name: Home-Run Bat
sections.card:
Summary: A wooden bat that changes your forward smash: you wind up and take one slow swing, which can knock an opponent out with a single hit.
Uses: Each swing takes the same amount of time, and you cannot charge it. In the first game it reuses each fighter's ordinary item swing, so the wind-up depends on who you play: Link needs only 23 frames, while Mario, Luigi and Ness need the most, at 30.
Tips: Hit with the end of the bat for the most damage, not the centre. Thrown, it is also strong, around 20% with big knockback, and ordinary swings can KO fairly early, above all a dash attack or a smash throw.

sections.name: Hammer
sections.card:
Summary: A short-range item: its holder keeps swinging it to and fro, and in the first game every hit does 30% with very high knockback.
Uses: In the series, holding it means you swing without pause and cannot use an air jump, any other attack or a shield. You cannot discard it by choice; only being knocked into a tumble makes you let go. The wiki says it can also follow up on itself for 60%, which will likely KO.
Tips: The item list names it among the items to fear most, because of its reach, damage and knockback. Still, in the series the person holding it has no special moves or air jump, so sending them off a ledge mid-swing can KO them. Carefully placed hitboxes can also cut the swing short.

sections.name: Ray Gun
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range laser gun with room for 16 shots. In the first game each shot deals 10% electric damage and knocks the target vertically.
Uses: You can fire one shot each 30 frames. Like the other shooting items it usually takes over your neutral attack, and when its ammo runs out it fires only blanks. The item list adds that its blasts have unlimited horizontal range.
Tips: A reflect or absorb move can handle the shots, while the gun itself can be reflected only when thrown. In the first two Smash games a fighter had to stand still while using a shooting item; Brawl was when firing on the move became possible.

sections.name: Bob-omb
sections.card:
Summary: A bomb on two stubby legs with a wind-up key sticking out of its back. Its blast does heavy damage and knockback, and it can catch the thrower too.
Uses: Pick it up and throw it at an opponent. The thrower can be hurt too, and any attack that hits it sets it off.
Tips: If nobody grabs it, the game's manual says it wanders off until its countdown reaches zero. In the series it then gets to its feet and paces to and fro along the platform where it appeared, turning at the edges; it goes off if it bumps into a fighter, and otherwise detonates by itself after a while.

sections.name: The 1P Game's final boss
sections.card:
Summary: The 1P Game's final boss, met in stage 11 on Final Destination. Knocking it past the edge of the stage does not clear the stage; only wearing down its 300 hit points does.
Weak points: No amount of knockback KOs Master Hand, and he is not pushed back by your hits, so draining his 300 hit points is the only way to win.
Looks like: A big hand in a glove.
Tips: Side Punch is a fist that drives across the stage for 20%. Big Swipe is a wide slap over the platform for 16%. Floor Sweep makes several passes over the stage at 12% per swipe. Power Punch hangs above you, then slams down in a burst of electricity. Below 100 HP, his Finger Bullet fires three pairs of Bullet Bills instead of one pair.

sections.name: Metal Mario
sections.card:
Summary: A sub-boss of the 1P Game's ninth stage, found solely on the Meta Crystal level. Few attacks make him flinch, he shrugs off grabs and throws while his damage is low, and his own hits knock you back unusually far.
Weak points: He resists launching until he has taken around 200% (this changes with difficulty), yet edge-guarding him works very well: once he is off the stage his huge falling speed wrecks his recovery. His 8-frame jumpsquat also makes his aerial attacks slow.
Looks like: A quick look makes him seem like Mario in a different outfit.
Tips: He does not dash and seldom jumps; he just walks steadily back and forth over the stage. On low difficulties he stays passive and tends to attack only after being interrupted, and he grows more aggressive and knocks harder as the setting rises. His behaviour is basic: mostly strolling left and right with an occasional attack.

sections.name: Giant Donkey Kong
sections.card:
Summary: A giant Donkey Kong that you meet in the 1P Game's sixth stage, on Congo Jungle, where two normal-sized computer partners help you fight.
Weak points: He can absorb up to about 300% before he can be launched, and his own hits knock harder and reach farther thanks to his size. That size also makes him an easier target, and his AI can be gamed into pacing along the top platform, although your partners often spoil the pattern by jumping into or attacking him.
Looks like: A Donkey Kong model scaled up to a far bigger size.
Tips: Look after your partners. If neither is KO'd you get the DK Defender bonus (10,000 points, 7,000 in the Japanese release), and if neither takes any damage you get the DK Perfect bonus (50,000 points). Higher difficulties make him play more like a level 9 computer fighter, while your partners stay at lower levels.

sections.name: Fighting Polygon Team
sections.card:
Summary: Thirty feeble purple polygon duplicates of the twelve fighters, met in stage 10 of the 1P Game on Duel Zone, with at most three on screen together.
Weak points: Being light, they usually fall to one hit, although higher difficulties make them heavier and tougher. Having no special moves cripples their recovery, and they cannot grab. They are passive too: mostly wandering the platforms and hardly ever attacking.
Looks like: Angular, glossy purple figures that for the most part follow the outline of the fighter they copy.
Tips: They collect items, and a throwing item usually gets thrown right away. In the bonus stage Race to the Finish they turn far more aggressive, chasing you as far as they can and attacking when you are within reach, and you cannot beat them there, nor can they KO you.

sections.name: Hyrule Castle's tornadoes (stage hazard)
sections.card:
Summary: Hyrule Castle, the stage where the 1P Game's first opponent Link waits, has four tornadoes that appear at random places; anyone they catch gets flung upward.
Weak points: A fighter inside a tornado can still be attacked. Land an aerial the moment they come out, and a meteor smash can drive them back in for more damage.
Tips: A tornado lasts roughly 10 to 20 seconds and wanders in a random direction, and it can abruptly accelerate and chase a fighter. Anyone caught is held for around two seconds, then flung up, which KOs somewhere from 65% to 130%, depending on weight and where the tornado is. In the 1P Game, a tornado KO on Link gives the Tornado Clear bonus of 3,000 points.

sections.name: Planet Zebes's rising acid (stage hazard)
sections.card:
Summary: Planet Zebes, where the 1P Game's eighth stage pits you against Samus, has acid that keeps rising and falling beneath it. Contact deals damage and heavy knockback, which can KO a fighter who already has high damage.
Weak points: The acid never climbs as far as the highest platform. A fighter knocked into it is shot upward, which gives a chance to use the recovery again, or to just drop back to the stage.
Tips: Holding a Starman, or anything else that strongly resists knockback, protects you from the acid; but if you drop past the stage's edge and into it while invincible, you self-destruct. Samus KO'd by the acid earns the Acid Clear bonus: 1,500 points (1,000 in the Japanese release).

sections.name: Sector Z's Arwings (stage hazard)
sections.card:
Summary: On Sector Z, where the 1P Game's third stage has you face Fox, Arwings sweep past and shoot lasers over the stage, dealing big damage and knockback.
Tips: Standing on an Arwing is risky: if it leaves the screen over the top or the side, you can be KO'd, and since Arwings often barrel roll or fly inverted, they effectively throw you off. You cannot stand on the Great Fox's main guns, and they never fire. Knocking Fox out with an Arwing earns the ARWING Clear bonus: 4,000 points (3,000 in the Japanese release). Sector Z is the biggest stage in the game.
